raw_case_text: A 57-year-old male geologist with history of cardiopulmonary sarcoidosis complicated by dilated cardiomyopathy presented approximately 8 months after OHT, with a 6-weeks history of diffuse painful, raised skin lesions and open sores of the hands. His immunosuppressive regimen consisted of a combination of methotrexate, leflunomide, tacrolimus, and 5 mg prednisone daily. Blood and skin cultures isolated Mycobacterium hemophilum. The patient was treated with intravenous antibiotics for 11 days when he developed complex partial seizures, headaches, blurry vision, and mood changes. Brain MRI with contrast demonstrated abnormal T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery signal hyperintensity in the cortical and subcortical right temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes without contrast enhancement (Figure 1). Susceptibility-weighted imaging sequences revealed innumerable chronic microhemorrhages in the bilateral infra- and supratentorial cerebral hemispheres. Early considerations included neurosarcoidosis, CNS infection, and lymphoma. However, cerebrospinal fluid studies were non-specific with two white blood cells, two red blood cells, glucose of 70, and mildly elevated protein of 47. Angiotensin-converting enzyme, meningoencephalitis PCR panel (including Escherichia coli K1, Haemophilus influenza, Listeria monocytogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Enterovirus, Herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, human herpesvirus 6, varicella zoster virus, parechovirus, and Cryptococcus neoformans/Cryptococcus gatii), Coccidioides and Cryptococcus antibodies, mycobacteria, viral and fungal cultures, flow cytometry, and cytology testing of the cerebrospinal fluid were unrevealing. Owing to disseminated mycobacterial infection, his immunosuppressive regimen was narrowed to tacrolimus (at goal level, 4-8 ng/ml) and prednisone 5 mg daily. Two weeks after discharge, the patient returned with progressively worsening gait ataxia. Repeat neuroimaging was significant for more extensive, confluent, non-enhancing right hemispheric white matter hyperintensities; and stable diffuse microhemorrhages (Figure 2). Spinal MR imaging was unremarkable. Right parietal leptomeningeal and cortex biopsy revealed changes consistent with CAA-ri. The vasculature showed presence of congophilic polarizable birefringent deposits, which stained strongly with anti-Abeta 6F/3D monoclonal antibody, and intramural and perivascular collections of histiocytes and lymphocytes (Figure 3). Tissue acid-fast and Gram stains were negative. Liquid chromatography-mass spectroscopy confirmed the presence of Abeta/A4 peptide deposition. Despite systemic mycobacterial infection, the pathological diagnosis of CAA-ri prompted immediate treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days followed by 60 mg oral prednisone. Steady clinical improvement followed shortly, and significant radiographic improvement was noted on repeat neuroimaging a month later (Figure 4). Subsequently, the decision was made to taper oral prednisone over 3 months, as mandated by the underlying systemic infection. No neurological recurrence was noted to date, at 6-months follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male orthotopic heart transplant recipient being treated for disseminated Mycobacterium haemophilum skin lesions developed acute complex partial seizures, headaches, blurry vision, mood changes, and progressive gait ataxia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Approximately 8 months after orthotopic heart transplantation for cardiopulmonary sarcoidosis, the patient presented with a 6-week history of diffuse painful raised skin lesions and open hand sores culture-positive for Mycobacterium haemophilum. Eleven days into IV antimycobacterial therapy, he developed complex partial seizures, headaches, blurred vision, and mood changes, followed 2 weeks after discharge by progressively worsening gait ataxia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Cardiopulmonary sarcoidosis complicated by dilated cardiomyopathy status post orthotopic heart transplantation 8 months prior; disseminated Mycobacterium haemophilum cutaneous/bloodstream infection; geologist by occupation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful raised skin lesions and hand sores, complex partial seizures, headaches, blurry vision, mood changes, and progressive gait ataxia. Home medications: methotrexate, leflunomide, tacrolimus, and prednisone 5 mg daily (narrowed to tacrolimus goal 4-8 ng/mL and prednisone 5 mg daily).

objective.physical_examination: Diffuse painful raised cutaneous lesions and open hand sores; neurological deterioration characterized by complex partial seizures, mood changes, and subsequent progressive gait ataxia.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood and skin lesion cultures grew Mycobacterium haemophilum.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial and 2-week repeat brain MRIs demonstrated confluent, non-enhancing T2/FLAIR white matter hyperintensities in the right temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes alongside innumerable chronic bilateral infra- and supratentorial microhemorrhages on SWI; spinal MRI was normal. Lumbar puncture CSF showed 2 WBCs, 2 RBCs, glucose 70 mg/dL, mildly elevated protein 47 mg/dL, normal ACE, negative flow cytometry and cytology, and negative meningoencephalitis PCR panel (including Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii), Coccidioides and Cryptococcus antibodies, and mycobacterial/viral/fungal cultures. Right parietal leptomeningeal and cortical biopsy demonstrated vascular congophilic polarizable birefringent amyloid deposits (strongly positive for anti-Abeta 6F/3D antibody and confirmed as Abeta/A4 peptide by LC-MS) with intramural and perivascular histiocytic and lymphocytic inflammation (negative Gram and AFB stains).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation (CAA-ri) co-occurring with disseminated Mycobacterium haemophilum infection in an orthotopic heart transplant recipient, confirmed by right parietal cortical/leptomeningeal biopsy histopathology, anti-Abeta immunohistochemistry, and LC-MS peptide identification; neurosarcoidosis, CNS lymphoma, and CNS infections (including M. haemophilum, Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, and Coccidioides) were excluded. Treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 5 days) followed by a 3-month oral prednisone taper (starting at 60 mg/day) alongside ongoing antimycobacterial therapy and narrowed immunosuppression (tacrolimus and low-dose prednisone), achieving steady clinical and MRI resolution with no recurrence at 6-month follow-up.
